subject: Chemistry
title: Cisplatin: Metal That Kills Cancer
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Cisplatin: Metal That Kills Cancer.

hook.text: Cisplatin contains platinum—the same metal in jewelry. It's one of the most widely used cancer drugs in the world.

buildup.text: In 1965, Barnett Rosenberg noticed bacteria stopped dividing near platinum electrodes. The platinum compound halted their growth.

discovery.text: Cisplatin cross-links DNA strands, preventing cells from copying their genetic code. Cancer cells die mid-division.

twist.text: Cisplatin cured Lance Armstrong's testicular cancer when it had spread to his brain and lungs—a near-miraculous recovery.

climax.text: Cisplatin treats bladder, lung, and ovarian cancers. Its cure rate for testicular cancer exceeds 90%.

punchline.text: A precious metal that cross-links DNA. Platinum jewelry saves lives as a cancer drug.

quiz.question: How was cisplatin's anti-cancer property discovered?
options: Bacteria stopped dividing near platinum electrodes in a laboratory experiment
Platinum miners showed unusually low cancer rates
A chemist accidentally injected platinum solution into a tumor

details.summary: Cisplatin is a platinum coordination compound that kills cancer cells by cross-linking DNA strands, preventing replication and triggering programmed cell death. Barnett Rosenberg discovered its anticancer properties accidentally in 1965 while studying the effects of electric fields on bacteria.
details.whyItMatters: Cisplatin cured testicular cancer, raising survival rates from less than 10 to over 95 percent. It remains a backbone chemotherapy drug used against ovarian, bladder, lung, and head and neck cancers.
takeaways: Cisplatin's platinum atom binds to DNA purine bases, creating cross-links
DNA cross-links block replication and trigger apoptosis in cancer cells
It transformed testicular cancer from often fatal to highly curable

faq.question: Why does cisplatin affect cancer cells more than normal cells?
faq.answer: Cancer cells divide rapidly and are more vulnerable to DNA damage because they have less time for repair. Cisplatin damages DNA in all cells, but fast-dividing cancer cells are more likely to encounter the damage during replication and trigger apoptosis. Normal cells repair more efficiently.

faq.question: Why does cisplatin cause such severe side effects like nausea and kidney damage?
faq.answer: Cisplatin is not selective for cancer cells. It damages DNA in all rapidly dividing tissues including the gut lining, causing nausea, and concentrates in the kidneys during excretion, causing nephrotoxicity. Aggressive hydration and anti-nausea medications help manage these effects.
